title: CCBE Guide on the Use of Generative AI by Lawyers
author: Council of Bars and Law Societies of Europe (CCBE)

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The CCBE accepts the cluster’s core view that GenAI offers use-case-dependent workflow benefits only when paired with informed human oversight, professional competence and safe deployment. It materially extends that position through detailed guidance on confidentiality, procurement, conflicts, cybersecurity and professional independence, while specifically identifying automation’s risk to junior-lawyer skill formation and calling for reinforced training.
qs: While there is potential for the GenAI tools to improve efficiency and support the delivery of legal advice and services, it is important to consider the risks associated with their use and their implications on lawyers’ professional obligations.

st.t: Supervised AI: Verification may consume efficiency gains
st.an: The CCBE accepts the supervised-aid model: lawyers remain accountable, must understand tool-specific limitations, apply use-case-sensitive verification and protect client data through concrete safeguards. st.t: AI filings: Disclosure rules divide otherwise similar courts
st.an: CCBE supports conditional GenAI assistance under continuing human professional responsibility. It treats existing duties—especially competence and confidentiality—as controlling, requires use-case-sensitive verification and technical understanding, and does not advocate blanket disclosure or prohibition. It does not materially develop the cluster’s comparative account of court-specific certification and filing regimes.
qs: Conclusion  While lawyers’ core professional obligations remain unchanged, the context in which they are applied is rapidly evolving due to technological advancements like GenAI.

st.t: Court governance: Assistive use retains human accountability
st.an: The CCBE supports the cluster’s principal proposition that generative AI remains assistive and does not displace lawyers’ professional accountability. It stresses that core obligations remain unchanged while their application must adapt to technological change, but the supplied evidence does not materially develop the cluster’s specific safeguards, task boundaries or court-governance mechanisms.
qs: Conclusion  While lawyers’ core professional obligations remain unchanged, the context in which they are applied is rapidly evolving due to technological advancements like GenAI.
This shifting landscape requires continuous reﬂection and adaptation to ensure that the core values of the legal profession are upheld amid new challenges and opportunities in legal practice.

st.t: Court responsibility: AI requires lifecycle supervision
st.an: The CCBE aligns with the cluster’s core view that GenAI does not displace existing human professional responsibility and that its evolving use requires continued adaptation. Its warnings about confidential-data exposure and fabricated legal material also support the need for verification and confidentiality safeguards, although it does not materially develop the cluster’s court-specific lifecycle governance model.

st.t: EU governance: Simplification tests enforceable safeguards
st.an: The CCBE guide supports the cluster’s risk-sensitive approach to AI governance. It describes differentiated EU obligations, separate GPAI requirements and continuing professional and general-law duties, while balancing anticipated benefits against confidentiality and hallucination risks. Its claims about efficiency and access to justice are prospective rather than evidence of regulatory effectiveness, consistent with the synthesis’s evidentiary caution.
qs: The AI Act establishes a risk-based framework that applies to all providers and users of AI systems in the EU market, regardless of origin.

st.t: Generative automation: Fluent work product still needs authority
st.an: CCBE aligns with the cluster’s core proposition: generative AI produces new content through probabilistic pattern recognition, but opaque processes and potentially misleading outputs make verification, confidentiality safeguards and compliance with lawyers’ existing professional obligations essential. Its contribution is qualitative professional guidance rather than task-performance evidence or broad transformation forecasts.
qs: Generative AI – the basics  2.1 Key characteristics of generative AI The key characteristic that differentiates GenAI systems from other AI systems is the production of new content in the form of text, image, audio or video.

For lawyers, this poses signiﬁcant challenges: ﬁrst, it makes it harder to verify and trust the accuracy and reliability of AI-generated content, which may compromise the quality of legal advice or submissions.

st.t: Justice access: Direct AI use shifts risk downward
st.an: The CCBE guide aligns with the synthesis’s balanced position: GenAI may improve efficiency, legal-service delivery and access to justice, but those benefits are conditional on safe deployment and compliance with professional obligations. Its warnings about confidentiality and fabricated legal outputs reinforce the synthesis’s reliability concerns, although it focuses primarily on lawyer-supervised use rather than directly examining unrepresented users’ limited verification capacity or the downward transfer of risk.
qs: It can also improve access to justice for those currently underserved.

st.t: Legal copilot: Verification costs define practical value

kp.k: Established professional obligations govern evolving AI use
kp.d: The CCBE presents professional-ethics guidance for lawyers, firms, Bars and Law Societies rather than an overarching framework for AI throughout the justice system. It argues that core obligations remain unchanged but require adaptation to changing technology, and expressly warns that its technological observations may become outdated even before publication.
qs: While lawyers’ core professional obligations remain unchanged, the context in which they are applied is rapidly evolving due to technological advancements like GenAI.
Similarly, this guide will also not cover the use of AI tools in the wider justice system but will focus on how lawyers use them and what they should and should not do.

kp.k: Reported adoption spans research, review and drafting
kp.d: The guide reports LexisNexis surveys conducted in March and July 2023 in the US, UK, France and Canada: 89% of lawyers were aware of GenAI, 41% had used it for any purpose and 15% for legal purposes. It separately attributes the leading actual or planned law-firm uses to the Thomson Reuters Institute's 2024 report; these are reported survey findings, not CCBE measurements of productivity.
qs: According to the International Legal Generative AI Report by LexisNexis (surveys conducted in March and July 2023 in the US, UK, France and Canada), 89% of lawyers were aware of GenAI, 41 % have used it for any purpose and 15% have used it for legal purposes.

A recent survey from Thomson Reuters Institute suggested that the top five use cases for law firms using or planning to use GenAI are legal research, document review, briefing or memo drafting, document summarisation and correspondence drafting.

kp.k: Productivity and access benefits remain conditional possibilities
kp.d: The CCBE identifies potential efficiency, research and quality improvements from safely configured and correctly used GenAI. Possible consequences include cost savings, faster cases, improved resource allocation, more strategic work and new specialisations. Better access to lawyers for underserved people is a separate prospective benefit; the guide does not establish realised savings or access gains.
qs: The use of GenAI in legal practice carries a long a list of potential benefits, provided it is set up and used correctly and safely.
This can lead to potential cost savings, faster processing of cases, better allocation of resources within the legal practice, and an increased focus on qualitative rather than routine tasks.
As such, GenAI has the potential to change the daily work routine of lawyers, making it possible, for example, to focus on strategic consulting and developing new specialisations.

kp.k: Embedded AI creates potentially unnoticed confidentiality exposure
kp.d: The guide warns that lawyers may unknowingly use GenAI through updates to everyday software. Translation tools, PDF readers and text editors can therefore create confidentiality risks even without deliberate adoption of a dedicated legal-AI product; the same care is required when handling client information through these tools.
qs: Users may not be aware that a functionality interacts with a GenAI model as this information is not made readily available in the options (menu) or elsewhere.
GenAI tools have increasingly been incorporated into many everyday tools which lawyers often use, such as translation tools, PDF readers, text editors or navigation apps.
The same care should be taken with conﬁdential information when using these tools.

kp.k: Client-data safeguards must precede entry into AI systems
kp.d: The CCBE warns that professional or data-protection breaches may occur at input, rather than only when information later leaks. Providers, employees and third parties may access data, while prompts and conversation histories may be retained or reused for training. It recommends withholding client-related data absent safeguards, reviewing provider terms and settings, and considering confidentiality contracts, zero retention, purpose-limited data protection agreements or locally controlled secure systems. Professional rules protect all client data, not merely personal data.
qs: the users themselves (i.e. lawyers) are responsible for the information they provide as an input to the system, and may be in breach of their professional obligations and/or relevant data protection laws already at the point of inputting the data into a system, for example as prompts.
refrain from entering any personal, conﬁdential, or other data related to the client into the user interface of the GenAI (e.g. as prompts/queries), unless there are appropriate safeguards in place.
The professional rules apply to all client data.

kp.k: Fabricated authorities and opacity undermine reliable legal work
kp.d: The guide describes risks of fabricated cases, judicial opinions and quotations, as well as invented principles and misrepresentations of jurisdiction-specific law. It cites reporting on sanctions incidents rather than a measured hallucination rate. It also argues that opaque model processes make accuracy and reliability harder to verify. Risk depends on the task, with requests for legal advice presented as more consequential than some other uses.
qs: In the context of legal services the GenAI output might produce entirely ﬁctional case law, create non-existent court cases or judicial opinions, falsely attribute quotes to judges or legal scholars or construct seemingly plausible but entirely invented legal arguments.
This means that even the developers and providers of these systems cannot fully explain how outputs are produced.
The risks discussed below depend on the use case, where some use cases involve signiﬁcant risks (e.g. asking for legal advice) while others may pose lesser risks.

kp.k: Competence requires technical understanding and contextual human verification
kp.d: The CCBE treats knowledge of professional technology as part of competence and retains lawyer responsibility for advice and representations. It recommends understanding capabilities, limitations and use-specific risks, pursuing training and consulting local professional guidance. Verification is qualified by use case: a footnote envisages certain risk-free tasks or recipients comprehensively informed about unverified output and its risks. Inappropriate reliance may expose lawyers to disciplinary sanctions, contempt, malpractice claims and damage to client interests and trust.
qs: Lawyers are responsible for their work, the advice they give and the representations they make (to the courts or other authorities).

The duty of competence of the lawyer is not only restricted to law and regulation, but encompasses the obligation to become knowledgeable about a technical product to be used for professional activities.
where the use case requires, verify the output of a GenAI before it is utilised in their work;
There may only be certain categories of tasks where it may be appropriate to utilise the output without the necessary veriﬁcation.

kp.k: Bias and automation complacency threaten independent judgment
kp.d: The CCBE argues that biased or excessively agreeable responses can displace critical, client-specific legal reasoning. Lawyers may internalise model biases, substitute automated conclusions for judgment or become dependent on a few providers' legal opinions. These are identified risks, especially where verification, quality control and independent legal analysis are insufficient, rather than demonstrated profession-wide effects.
qs: Consequently, the AI may prioritise generating agreeable responses over providing accurate or critical information, potentially leading to misleading or unbalanced outputs.
Another risk that arises in this context is overreliance on outputs, which can lead to ‘automation complacency’ and substituting human judgment with automated conclusions.
The risk is ampliﬁed where there is insufficient quality control and veriﬁcation of the accuracy of the output, and insufficient independent legal analysis by the lawyer.

kp.k: Client disclosure depends on reasonably anticipated reservations
kp.d: The guidance does not prescribe universal disclosure of every AI use. It recommends transparency where an informed client could reasonably be expected to object, impose conditions or have reservations about the particular use. It also notes divergent client demands, including demands to use AI and demands not to use it.
qs: As with other technologies and tools, if it can reasonably be assumed that an informed client would object, make conditions, or otherwise have reservations in respect of use of the GenAI for the purpose in question, the lawyer should make sure to be transparent with the client.
While some clients may demand the use of AI tools from their lawyers, other clients may demand from their lawyers not to use any AI tools at all, in particular not GenAI.

kp.k: Shared client information creates conflict risks within firms
kp.d: The CCBE warns that AI access to multiple clients' confidential information can cause inadvertent sharing or conflicts, including inside a single firm. Its illustrative scenario concerns retained data from a former client being used by AI in a current client's case against that former client; a locally contained system therefore does not itself eliminate conflict concerns.
qs: The use of GenAI by lawyers can create risks for maintaining conﬂicts of interest obligations because AI systems may be trained on or have access to conﬁdential information from multiple clients within the law ﬁrm, potentially leading to inadvertent information sharing or conﬂicts.
If the client data of client B is still stored in the law ﬁrm and used by the AI system, it may be that its own client data is used in a case against them.

kp.k: AI regulation supplements jurisdiction-specific professional duties
kp.d: The guide describes GenAI as falling within existing AI-system definitions, often also general-purpose categories, rather than a separately defined category under the EU AI Act. It discusses risk-based regulation, general data-protection obligations and the Council of Europe framework alongside professional rules. It specifically reports an Article 4 AI-literacy requirement applying from 2 February 2025 to organisations acting as providers or users.
qs: The use of AI systems, including GenAI, by lawyers is usually subject to the professional obligations applicable in a given jurisdiction and to other laws to which lawyers would normally be subject.

For example, in the EU, starting from 2 February 2025, the AI Act (under Article 4) requires all organisations to ensure their staff are knowledgeable about AI, regardless of whether they are involved in the AI value chain as providers or users (also referred to as ‘deployers’ in the EU AI Act).

kp.k: Cybersecurity and synthetic fraud require broader safeguards
kp.d: The guide identifies more sophisticated phishing, prompt injection, data poisoning and model poisoning as risks to legal practices and AI output integrity. Deepfakes and synthetic identities may facilitate impersonation, fake documents and manipulation of identification systems. Future questions about counterfeit law firms and live witness testimony are explicitly posed as issues for monitoring and response, not established incidents.
qs: GenAI tools may also introduce new attack vectors.
Other cybersecurity risks include data or source corruption (called data poisoning) or model poisoning, both of which may compromise the GenAI tool’s behaviour and outputs (e.g. feedback loops).
Potential risks include producing fake documents, impersonation or manipulating facial recognition systems which can result in reputational harms or leaking of sensitive information.
How would lawyers detect and respond to deep-faked online live testimonies of witnesses?

kp.k: Junior-task automation could erode professional formation
kp.d: The CCBE anticipates a training problem if drafting and review previously assigned to juniors are automated. It recommends reinforcing affected skills and retaining education in underlying legal tasks, alongside training in tool operation, questioning and error avoidance. This is a prospective formation concern, not evidence of measured junior displacement or a forecast of a particular staffing structure.
qs: Therefore, it is essential that the training of lawyers in the performance of the underlying tasks should not be neglected.

If the work which was traditionally given to junior lawyers to train them in drafting and review is automated, a new light is thrown on training such lawyers, and consideration should be given to ensuring that their training is reinforced in those areas where their skills might otherwise be eroded.

kp.k: Vendor concentration may challenge professional self-regulation
kp.d: As a future consideration, the guide questions whether dependence on a small number of powerful technology providers able to impose contractual conditions could affect the legal profession's collective independence. It also flags procurement questions about where and how tools were developed, without offering evidence that professional self-regulation has already been displaced.
qs: Gen AI tools, and other technologies, are to a large extent developed and marketed by a relatively small number of technology providers that together hold considerable market power and can impose conditions on the use of their services.
Therefore, there arises a question whether the independence of the profession as a whole could be affected;

kp.k: Lawyers' published expertise may train competing AI services
kp.d: The CCBE argues that scraping publicly accessible case analyses, legislative guides and research can turn firms' intellectual work into AI training material. It predicts that resulting products might compete with lawyers without equivalent professional obligations, and recommends vigilance over public publication. Separately, it flags copyright risks, provider terms permitting input reuse or claiming output ownership, and trade-secret claims that restrict transparency; these are concerns and possibilities rather than a settled account of rights in every output.
qs: For law ﬁrms, this means their intellectual assets – such as case analyses, legislative guides, and specialised research publications – are being harvested and integrated into AI training datasets.
These may in the future develop solutions that would challenge the services provided by lawyers while not being subject to the same professional obligations and in effect, remaining unregulated.
Some agreements may note that the AI provider and vendor retains ownership of the output data.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The CCBE describes increasing lawyer adoption of GenAI, including potentially unnoticed adoption through ordinary software updates.
pts.d: Section 3.1 identifies research, document review, briefing or memo drafting, summarisation and correspondence as prominent uses or intended uses. The CCBE also reports growth in specialised legal research and drafting tools trained on or linked to legal data. It warns that users may not realise that newly integrated features interact with GenAI.

pts.k: The CCBE anticipates efficiency, research and quality improvements that could reduce costs and shift lawyers toward higher-value work.
pts.d: Section 3.2 presents these as potential benefits, conditional on correct and safe setup and use, rather than measured outcomes. Examples include automated document creation, rapid analysis of large document collections, more accurate research, error reduction, compliance checking and standardised processes. Potential downstream changes include faster cases and client responses, better workload-based cost estimates, resource allocation, strategic consulting and new specialisations.

pts.k: The CCBE suggests GenAI could improve access to lawyers and justice for underserved people.
pts.d: The guide separates this prospective access benefit from ordinary client-service and practice-efficiency improvements. It does not specify an implementation model, estimate the reduction in unmet legal need or provide an access-to-justice outcome study.

pts.k: The CCBE warns that fabricated legal material and opaque outputs can compromise advice and submissions, making human verification central to responsible use.
pts.d: Sections 3.3 and 4.2 describe fabricated cases, quotations and legal propositions, and difficulties checking AI-generated content. Lawyers retain responsibility for their work; insufficient verification can expose them to sanctions, malpractice litigation and reputational damage while harming clients and trust. The source generally frames AI as lawyer-supervised assistance, not a transfer of professional responsibility to a system.

pts.k: The CCBE identifies new confidentiality, data-protection and conflicts risks when client information enters shared or vendor-operated AI systems.
pts.d: The guide says a professional or data-protection breach may occur at input, before any output is used. Depending on system arrangements, providers may retain prompts, reuse information for training, access input and output, or share information with third parties. Cross-client information use may create conflicts even within a single firm: the guide hypothetically describes stored information from a former client being used against that client. These are conditional risks, not documented incidents in the guide.

pts.k: The CCBE warns that bias, sycophancy, automation complacency and dependence on concentrated technology suppliers could undermine professional independence.
pts.d: At the individual level, lawyers may internalise biased or overly agreeable recommendations and substitute automated conclusions for independent legal analysis. At the profession-wide level, a small number of powerful providers can impose service conditions. The CCBE raises the resulting threat to collective independence and self-regulation as a question requiring monitoring, not an established outcome.

pts.k: The CCBE predicts changes to competence and training requirements and warns that automating junior work could erode professional skills.
pts.d: The guide treats understanding technical tools as part of current professional competence. Looking ahead, it suggests that questioning GenAI effectively and understanding its errors may become essential training. If drafting and review traditionally assigned to juniors are automated, training must preserve the underlying legal skills. This is a conditional training concern, not a quantified claim about junior job losses or staffing structures.

pts.k: The CCBE claims that publicly accessible law-firm knowledge is becoming AI training material and could help create competing services.
pts.d: Section 5 describes case analyses, legislative guides and specialised publications as intellectual assets harvested for training. It predicts that AI companies may use such material to develop solutions challenging lawyers' services without equivalent professional obligations. The guide does not identify a specific resulting competitor, quantify market displacement or demonstrate that such competition has already occurred.

pts.k: The CCBE anticipates more difficult security and fraud problems and divergent client demands about AI use.
pts.d: The guide describes more sophisticated phishing, prompt injection and data or model poisoning as risks. It identifies deepfake impersonation and synthetic identities as threats, while posing law-firm impersonation and deepfaked live witness testimony as future questions rather than documented events. Separately, it says clients increasingly recognise AI opportunities and risks; some may demand AI use and others prohibit it, making transparency relevant when an informed client could reasonably have reservations.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The guide combines adoption surveys, professional authority, illustrative sanctions and copyright cases, vendor policies and secondary technical sources; most benefits and structural predictions are not empirically quantified.
pts.d: Adoption: the CCBE cites LexisNexis surveys conducted in March and July 2023 across the US, UK, France and Canada, and Thomson Reuters Institute's 2024 survey of uses or intended uses. Benefits: Thomson Reuters respondents' expectations support the discussion, not measured productivity or quality improvements. Reliability: footnote 22 cites Reuters reporting on New York lawyers sanctioned over fabricated ChatGPT cases and a February 2025 ABA Journal report about possible sanctions over AI citations; these illustrate incidents, not model error rates. Confidentiality: references include provider privacy policies, Docusign FAQs, commentary and CCBE cloud guidance. Professional duties: the CCBE Charter and Model Code supply normative authority. Copyright and competition: footnote 34 cites copyright litigation involving OpenAI and Microsoft, the Thomson Reuters–Ross Intelligence ruling and creative-industry objections; these are contextual support, not evidence of law-firm market displacement. No original experiment, performance benchmark or quantified forecast is presented.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The 2 October 2025 guide distinguishes current use and immediate obligations from undated longer-term risks; benefits and harms depend heavily on use case and safeguards.
pts.d: The numerical adoption evidence is from 2023, not a 2025 prevalence estimate. Current risks are qualified by task, system design, data handling and oversight. Advice generation is described as higher-risk than some other tasks. Confidential client input is discouraged unless appropriate contractual, data-protection or technical safeguards exist. Verification is required where the use case requires it; footnote 32 allows limited possibilities for risk-free tasks or comprehensively informed recipients. Independence, competition and skill erosion have no specified forecast horizon. The source explicitly warns that its technical observations may become outdated.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are practising lawyers and firms, junior lawyers, clients, underserved people, professional bodies and technology suppliers.
pts.d: Lawyers and firms may gain efficiency and strategic capacity while retaining liability and assuming tool-selection, training, security and verification responsibilities. Juniors face potential loss of drafting and review learning opportunities. Existing and former clients face confidentiality, conflict and advice-quality risks; clients may also receive faster, cheaper or more accessible services. Underserved people are potential access-to-justice beneficiaries. Bars and Law Societies face guidance, education and independence questions. Technology suppliers may gain influence and competitive products from legal content. Courts and public confidence are affected through the quality and integrity of lawyers' submissions, although the guide expressly excludes broader justice-system AI use from its main scope. No firm-size or practice-market breakdown of effects is supplied.
